title: Injuries among weightlifters and powerlifters: a systematic review
authors: Aasa U, Svartholm I, Andersson F, Berglund L
population: Olympic weightlifters and powerlifters in 9 studies of injury incidence and prevalence; competitive lifters, not recreational runners
findings: Five databases were searched in March and April 2015 and 9 studies were included; the authors rate most of them as of low methodological quality.
The spine, shoulder and knee were the most common injury locations in both sports.
Injury incidence was 2.4-3.3 injuries per 1000 hours of training in weightlifting and 1.0-4.4 per 1000 hours in powerlifting. Only one retrospective study had analysed risk factors.

The authors conclude that the risk of injury in both sports was similar to other non-contact sports that require strength and power and low compared with contact sports, and that the severity of injuries differed between studies.
limitations: Competitive lifters training for maximal lifts, not recreational runners lifting submaximal loads; nine studies, most of low quality, mostly retrospective; no data on a beginner learning a barbell lift. It describes the injury rate of a sport, not the risk of a first barbell session. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: The only injury-rate data for barbell lifting in the corpus, from competitive lifters. It lets the plan say that injury rates in these sports are in the range of other non-contact sports, and it says nothing about a recreational runner starting a squat or a hinge: the controls (a safety line, no maximal attempt, repetitions left in the first session) stay.
Upper limit of what the app can say: no statement that barbell lifts are safe for runners.
